Shipped, stress-broken, then hardened · 5 September 2026

Fork the board, edit privately, Compare, then Merge — or Rebase.

The Draft+Version model the 2026-09-03 research report selected is a working product surface, rebuilt from scratch against current main. A Drafts chip sits in the top-left shell, deliberately left of the breadcrumb; opening a draft adds a bar that pushes the canvas down; Compare reuses the existing Figma-style diff engine scoped to Draft vs Main; and a GitHub-style Merge ▾ split button's chevron reveals Rebase — pulling Main's current edits into the draft, the inverse of Merge. An earlier build of this page called that finished. Then a recorded user session and two independent review passes — a correctness stress test and a UX audit, both driving the running app — found a broken rename, two real data-loss bugs, and a dozen smaller gaps. All of it is fixed, and this page now tells the whole story: what shipped, what broke, how each break was closed, and what proves it stays closed.

2 data-loss bugs found by stress-testing the reported rename bug, root-caused twice Merge is fail-closed now Rebase merges fields, not whole records Compare engine reused, not forked Main's file never touched by a draft

What it looks like

All four captures are the running app in a real browser on 2026-09-05, taken after the fix pass — the draft bar is a real chrome row, and the two thin strips show behavior the first version got wrong.

What a real test session found

A 10.2-second recorded session (recordings/2026-09-05_16-21-02-take/) produced one user-reported bug: “I tried to double-click the text to rename it there, but wasn't able to.” Two independent passes followed — a correctness stress test over complex board content (Branch regions, Loops, Behavior Trees, Definition-linked Blocks) and a UX audit driving the live app — and both converged on the same root causes. None of this was found by re-reading the code.

Merge silently destroyed concurrent edits to Main Found by the stress test · a real data-loss bug in the version this report first called finished

The break

Merge wrote the draft's snapshot over Main wholesale, with no check at all. An edit made to Main while the draft was open — a peer session, another window, an edit from before the draft was resumed — was destroyed with no diff, no undo entry on the other side, and a success report.

The fix

Merge is fast-forward only and fail-closed: at the instant of the click it re-reads Main fresh from disk (readMainDrift, never the cached flag or fork-point slot) and refuses if Main has drifted at all, pointing at Rebase one click away. An unreadable Main also refuses — “check failed” never falls through to “overwrite”.

draft_merge_guard_smoke.mjs replays the exact repro: an unrelated on-disk edit to Main survives the refused merge (beta w=654 still on disk), and Rebase-then-Merge lands both sides' work.

Rebase could report success while reverting Main's edit Found by the stress test · the second data-loss bug, and the deeper design flaw

The break

Rebase asked “what changed” twice, at two different granularities. Conflict detection ran through compareBoards — the display diff behind the badge, which deliberately ignores position — while the merge overlay ran on a raw whole-record diff, which sees it. A draft that only moved a shape Main had independently renamed was invisible to the conflict check but visible to the overlay: the draft's entire stale record was copied over Main's rename, and the rebase reported success. A display diff was deciding what was safe to overwrite.

The fix

The merge logic was rewritten, not patched: one complete, field-by-field comparison (fieldViewOf — every top-level key plus one level into props, the unit this app actually writes) drives both halves of the decision. Two edits to different fields of one record — a move and a rename, a retitle and a port addition — now merge, keeping both; two edits to the same field still block; delete-vs-edit stays a whole-record refusal. compareBoards keeps its job of describing changes to a human and has no say in what gets written — the whole point of draftRebase.ts's module header.

12 unit cases in draftRebase.test.ts pin it down — the same-record-different-fields cases are merges the shipped version refused by construction, so reverting the fix fails them outright — and the journey proves the literal repro closed: x=640, y=480, props.w=777 all surviving on one record.

Behavior Tree boards could never have rebased Found in the same pass · an unrelated latent bug the two-diff gap had been hiding

The break

The Behavior Tree projection minted a fresh random definitionId for every projected Block on every reconcile — every load, every XML edit — via getDefaultBlockProps(). Its documented idempotency (“a second call with nothing changed writes nothing”) was quietly false, and under the new raw field-level diff, draft and Main each roll their own ids: every leaf reads as a same-field conflict, so any board containing a Behavior Tree would have been permanently unable to Rebase.

The fix

projectedBlockDefaults() simply omits the field: an existing leaf keeps whatever id it was persisted with (a spread cannot overwrite a key it does not carry), and a brand-new leaf is stamped once by installDefinitionLinking's beforeCreate handler — the same one-time mint every hand-drawn Block gets. Not a path-derived id, which would silently link two regions showing the same tree into one Definition. behaviorTreeProjectionIdentity.test.ts asserts byte-identical re-projection under both lenses.

Double-clicking a draft's name corrupted it The user-reported bug — independently root-caused by both reviews to the same cause

The break

A single click already swaps the name into an editable, auto-selected input — by design, matching the file-title rename. A habitual double-click's second click lands ~100–200ms later on the now-different, freshly-mounted input: an ordinary click inside a focused text field, which collapses the just-made selection to a bare caret. Typing then inserts mid-word (“Draft 1” → “DraNew nameft 1”), committing silently on blur. No native dblclick ever fires — the two clicks hit different elements.

The fix

The input records when it mounted and swallows a stray mousedown within 400ms — a rapid second click leaves the selection intact so typing replaces the name, while a deliberate slow click still places a caret normally. Fixed at both sites the pattern exists (the bar's name and the popover's per-row rename), per the house rule of fixing the sibling paths, and draft_ux_polish_smoke.mjs drives real timed rapid clicks at each, asserting the committed name is exactly what was typed.

Twelve more findings from the UX audit

The audit drove the live app and filed 15 findings in all; the three above were the deep ones. The twelve below were fixed in the same pass — each fix verifiable in the diff or a journey.

FindingFix
A move-only draft was permanently stuck — the change count that gated Merge and Rebase is structurally blind to position, so both buttons disabled forever (same root-cause class as the Rebase bug). Enablement gates on hasUnpromotedEdits — a raw digest of the draft's stored content — never on changes.total. Proven in the move-only journey step above.
Merge fired on one unconfirmed click with no way back — asymmetric with Discard's two-step confirm. First a two-step confirm on the button; now superseded by the review dialog below, which shows the diff being applied instead of restating it in a label.
A refused Merge produced no feedback at all. A status line distinguishes “Main has N changes… Rebase first” from “could not check Main” — only one of them points at an action.
The “Main changed since this draft” banner was computed once at draft-entry and never refreshed — it could claim either calm or conflict long after reality changed. Re-settled at every moment the answer matters: entering/resuming a draft, opening Compare, both Rebase outcomes, and a refused Merge. Still advisory only — merge() never trusts it.
The Compare button's badge and the dialog it opened answered two different questions (confirmed live: button “1 Change”, dialog “0 Added · 2 Removed · 1 Modified”). Both now computed from the same two snapshots — fresh Main vs the live head — so they cannot disagree.
Entering a draft snapped the canvas down with a hard layout jump. The canvas wrapper animates its height (180ms), with a prefers-reduced-motion opt-out.
Every draft claimed “based on v0.1” even though no version has ever been pinned — a fabricated label. Truthful “based on Main · 2m ago” until a version actually exists; the real label once one does.
Escape inside the popover's rename input closed the whole popover instead of canceling the rename. The rename's Escape stops propagation past Radix's dismissable layer; cancel and close are separate.
Draft rows read as one run-on accessible name (“Draft 1based on v0.1”), and icon-only buttons had no names. Explicit aria-labels throughout; the rename inputs gained aria-describedby help text.
Committing an empty rename silently reverted to the old name. “Give this draft a name.” shown inline, focus kept in the field — both rename sites.
Row action buttons were 22×22px, under the 24px minimum target size, with contrast gaps beside them. Targets enlarged and tokens adjusted in drafts.css (the 22×22 case is called out in the file).
Compare's changed-element rows were anonymous — a Block, a cable and a rectangle all looked the same. Per-kind glyphs and inline ADDED/EDITED badges in the element list (visible in the capture above).

Then Merge and Rebase became reviews

Zach, watching the two-step confirm: “instead of doing a double click confirmation, whenever you click that, then it will again open essentially the compare view — however in maybe a slightly altered state, where maybe you can accept or not accept for now each modification.” The reference was IcePanel's own Merge changes modal.

Both entry points keep their exact position and label. What changed is what the click does: it opens the Compare dialog the app already has, through one more optional prop on the same component — the identical move that let drafts reuse it for Draft-vs-Main in the first place. With no action the dialog renders byte-for-byte as it always has, which is what keeps the Shift+D history path unchanged (proved below, by re-running its three journeys).

How it's built

Three seams carry the whole feature. Everything else — the diff engine, the board renderer, autosave, the chrome — was already there.

Autosave holdOne boolean, 5 guards

draftHoldRef in LocalWorkspace.tsx mirrors the existing protectedRef quarantine pattern: while a draft is open it gates every path that could write Main's .systemsketch file. Draft edits autosave to localStorage instead, via the provider's own debounced listener.

The Rebase journey proves the seal: it diffs Main's file bytes on disk before and after draft edits and after the Rebase click — identical every time.

CompareGeneralized, not forked

One optional source?: CompareExplicitSource — two labeled snapshots — threads through useCompare().open() into the 1,130-line dialog. With a source it seeds both sides directly, skips version discovery, and swaps the History rail for a two-line header. Without one, nothing changed: compareModel.ts, BoardRender, PropertyTable and CodeView are untouched, and the three pre-existing Compare smoke journeys still pass on the Shift+D history path.

RebaseOne question, one granularity

computeRebase is pure: raw record-level diffs (fork-point→Main, fork-point→draft) decide what each side touched, and a record both sides touched gets a field-level three-way merge — only a field both sides moved differently is a conflict. The candidate result must then survive a referential-integrity sweep: every binding's fromId/toId and every shape's non-page parentId must resolve, so Main deleting a Block the draft wired a cable to still blocks.

Any conflict blocks with a message pointing at Compare. No resolution UI — a conflict is a refusal, in both directions, and the display diff has no say in what gets written.

Known trade-offs, kept deliberately

Named in the plan before building, re-checked after the fix pass. None of these is hidden behind the green numbers below.

Main's external-change polling is suspended while a draft is open.

The idle-poll guard that must ignore draft-local edits cannot also watch Main's file. Acceptable for a single-user local app — and after the fix pass this is compensated everywhere it matters: Compare, Rebase and now Merge itself re-read Main fresh from disk at the moment of the action, never from a cached fork-point slot, which is exactly what turned the blind overwrite into a refusal.

A few hundred milliseconds of draft edits can be lost on an abrupt tab close.

The draft's localStorage autosave is debounced, and the browser's unsaved-changes warning is intentionally suppressed while the hold is active. The same window the prototype had — not widened, and deliberately not closed now.

Versions stay metadata-only.

Merging pins a VersionRecord — label, name, timestamp — with no retained content and no non-destructive restore. The fuller IcePanel versioning model from the research report was not requested for this pass. What did change: the UI no longer pretends otherwise — the fabricated “based on v0.1” row label is gone until a version is actually pinned.

Try it

The review board below was generated through the real editor and driven once in the app. Its callout texts are read verbatim from the fixture recipe at build time.

1 · Click Drafts in the top-left shell, then New draft
2 · Rename Planner to "Planner v2" in the inspector — the bar's Compare count becomes 1
3 · Click Compare 1 Change. This stays a PURE review: no checkboxes, no confirm bar, nothing to press.
4 · Close it, then click Merge — ONE click, no arming. The SAME dialog reopens, titled "Merge changes", every changed element ticked, with "› Merge 1 change" at the bottom right. Untick Planner v2: the confirm greys out and says applying only some changes isn't supported yet.
5 · Re-tick it and close. Now click the chevron beside Merge, then Rebase. The right-hand board is captioned "<draft> (after Rebase)" — the draft as it WOULD look, computed before anything is applied. Confirming runs the real Rebase.
PASS WHEN · Compare opens with NO checkboxes and NO bottom bar · Merge and Rebase each open the same dialog with a per-element tick and one confirm · unticking anything disables the confirm and explains why instead of quietly applying everything · the Rebase review's after-board is the proposed draft, not Main · confirming Merge writes to Main and closes the dialog; a Main that moved underneath refuses IN the dialog and leaves both sides intact
